title: Diet Drinks or Water? A Two-Year Weight Study
paragraphs: Many people choose diet soft drinks to cut sugar, but some worry that sweeteners might increase appetite and make weight loss harder. A two-year study from the universities of Liverpool and Leeds, published in the British Journal of Nutrition, suggests this is not the case.

The SWITCH trial followed 493 adults with overweight or obesity who took part in a structured weight-loss programme. They were randomly asked to drink either water or diet drinks every day. In the final year, they no longer received support from the programme.

After two years, people in the diet drink group had lost an average of 4.8 kilos and those in the water group 3.7 kilos. Because the difference was not statistically significant, the researchers concluded that diet drinks were about as effective as water. However, the study was funded by the American Beverage Association, and critics point out that many participants left the study early.

questions.q: What worry about sweeteners did the study test?
questions.a: That they might increase appetite and make weight loss harder.

questions.q: What changed in the final year?
questions.a: Participants no longer received support from the programme.

questions.q: Give two reasons why some people are careful about the results.
questions.a: The drinks industry funded it, and many participants left the study early.
